title: Should You Keep Misbehaving Students Out Of Fun Activities? -of-fun-activities/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Addressing a recurring reader question, Linsin recommends removing teacher discretion from the decision of whether misbehaving students participate in fun activities. He advises laying out participation conditions in advance—within an elementary time-out plan, a student who is in time-out when an activity begins simply remains there until requirements are met, with nothing changing based on the activity. For special events like parties, he recommends writing specific criteria into the classroom management plan or a separate document sent home for parents to sign well ahead of time. This up-front documentation removes ambiguity and prevents arguments, positioning the teacher as an impartial referee rather than a decision-maker. The result, he argues, is that students who miss out reflect on their own choices rather than blaming the teacher, and the teacher avoids being perceived as either unfair or a pushover.
points: The teacher should not make an in-the-moment decision about excluding misbehaving students from fun activities; the rule should be set in advance.
Under an elementary time-out plan, a student in time-out when an activity starts simply stays in time-out until requirements are met—nothing changes for the activity.
For special events, participation conditions should be written into the classroom management plan or a document parents sign ahead of time.
Laying out conditions in advance removes the teacher from the equation, turning them into an impartial referee rather than a decision-maker.
This approach causes students who miss an activity to reflect on their own misbehavior rather than blame the teacher for being unfair.
quotes: It’s an option that removes the guesswork and places the decision of whether or not you allow them to participate with the student .
If a student is in time-out when the activity begins, then they remain in time-out. That is, until they meet the time and behavior requirements needed to rejoin their classmates.
You’re just a referee calling ’em like you see ’em, continuing to be consistent regardless of the activity.
Put it in writing as part of your classroom management plan and syllabus or information packet you send home for parents to sign.
Get everyone on record ahead of time so there are no arguments or misunderstandings. Turn the responsibility of whether and how much they participate over to your students.
It also removes the possibility of your students seeing you as either unfair . . . Or a pushover.
